transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay great, hi everyone, I'm Maya from Redwood, thanks for joining. We have Luis from SE and Hannah from solutions, and we want to walk through the Optimize playbook for prefetch and batching for VerdantBridge.
[00:08] Aisha Khan: Hi, thanks. Our goal is to drop per-token cost by at least 30% on peak while keeping p95 under 450 ms. We have a hybrid conversational/search product.
[00:16] Luis Ortega: Perfect. Can you remind us of your current footprint — model size, approximate QPS, session length?
[00:22] Tom Reed: Right now we run an open-weights 13B on GpuPools (self-hosted). Peak QPS around 120 RPS across two regions, average session maybe 8 turns, but some long sessions to 40 turns for power users.
[00:36] Maya Chen: Good. So a few quick goals for today — show Optimize console suggestions, run through prefetch/prefix cache vs session-KV tradeoffs, and model out three cost scenarios. We'll reference the workbook I uploaded.
[00:46] Priya Menon: Quick note on security: we use customer KMS and strict RBAC, everything has to be auditable.
[00:52] Hannah Park: That's fine, the Private/KMS notes are in the security pack, we'll share the doc link.
[00:57] Luis Ortega: Jumping into the console — //screen share noise// you'll see the Optimize tab. First panel is Workload summary, it ingests heatmaps — session length, token distribution. For VerdantBridge the tail is heavy, which is why lookahead or prefix prefetch will help.
[01:15] Aisha Khan: Can you define lookahead again? Is that the KV prefetch we discussed?
[01:20] Luis Ortega: Yes, sometimes called prefix or lookahead: when a session is active we precompute KV cache for likely next tokens or prompts so that subsequent calls bypass full attention compute. Helps when sessions have predictable drift, like guided flows or search context.
[01:33] Tom Reed: Are there storage costs for that? We have concerns about KV storage and evictions.
[01:38] Luis Ortega: Good point — Optimize proposes TTLs and adaptive eviction. We model storage as a small per-GB cost in the workbook, and you can set a ttl per-key. The tradeoff is TTL too long -> wasted storage and stale cache, TTL too short -> misses.
[01:51] Maya Chen: For your workload we recommended a hybrid: session-affine KV for active users (short TTL, 5–15 minutes) plus prefix prefetch for common flows (longer TTL for flow IDs). That reduces recompute without blowing up storage. See sheet tab 'VD-hybrid-1'.
[02:05] Tom Reed: I see the workbook, nice. The conservative scenario still saves 18% on tokens, balanced 34%, aggressive 52% — are those realistic?
[02:15] Luis Ortega: They are based on our empirical sims with your QPS distribution you shared; aggressive assumes high cache hit (0.65) for prefixes and good batching at 2–3x dynamic batch factor. Conservative assumes low hit ~0.3. These are sensitive to session churn.
[02:29] Priya Menon: On batching — what's the main config? We currently do fixed-size batches at the service level.
[02:34] Luis Ortega: Optimize recommends dynamic batching with size-adaptive windows: you let a short micro-window (10–12 ms) and a longer window for slow tail. We also recommend shaping concurrency — allow more inflight short requests to fill batches and keep p95 targets by capping per-tenant concurrency.
[02:50] Aisha Khan: So is there a risk that batching will increase p95?
[02:53] Luis Ortega: There's always a latency vs cost tradeoff. The console has a latency SLO slider — you can set p95 target 450 ms, and Optimize will suggest batch window and concurrency cap to meet it while maximizing batch size. It balances warm vs cold starts and prefetch hit rates.
[03:09] Tom Reed: How does warmup behave for model variants or quantized models?
[03:12] Hannah Park: Warmup is twofold: kernel warmup (first token costs) and KV warm cache. For quantized weights we sometimes see slightly different per-token throughput; Optimize's runtime profile chooses kernels accordingly. We usually recommend a brief warmup wave when deploying a new variant — we can do canary rollouts with hitless fallback.
[03:29] Aisha Khan: About fallbacks — we need graceful degradation to a cheaper model if capacity spikes.
[03:34] Maya Chen: Yup, routing policies allow fallback to a less expensive quantized variant or even to our hosted fallback with a cost ladder. That can be automated by load or latency triggers.
[03:41] Tom Reed: Any notes about multi-region sync for KV? Our sessions can cross regions.
[03:45] Luis Ortega: For cross-region sessions we recommend session affinity plus a small replication window for KV of hot sessions (eventual consistency). Alternatively, route the session to a single region via sticky routing — that reduces cross-region write/read costs. We'll put both scenarios in the sandbox test plan.
[03:59] Aisha Khan: On security again: KMS integrations — do you support customer-managed keys and HSM?
[04:04] Maya Chen: Yes — Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and we have audit logs streamed to your SIEM. We'll attach the SOC2/ISO doc.
[04:11] Caleb Ortiz: About observability: we need per-request token-level cost and a way to attach traces to internal request ids.
[04:16] Hannah Park: Console exposes per-route cost breakdown, token buckets, and tracing hooks you can turn on for specific routes — it can export to Jaeger/Tempo.
[04:24] Tom Reed: Let's dig into the cost model assumptions — what does the workbook assume for GPU hourly, token egress, and storage?
[04:29] Luis Ortega: In the workbook we use regional pricing bands: GPU equivalent hourly for a reserved pool, a per-token egress + embedding price, and storage at $0.02/GB/mo for KV. We also model reserved vs burst capacity — reserved reduces per-token compute by ~20% in our examples.
[04:44] Aisha Khan: Can you open the scenario where prefix hit rate is 0.6 and batch factor is 2.5?
[04:49] Maya Chen: //scrolling// that's 'VD-hybrid-2' tab. It shows per-day token consumption, compute-hours, and net savings. Note the effect of sessionization — if your session affinity increases by 15% we get an extra 8% savings.
[05:03] Priya Menon: Which metrics should we capture during sandbox to validate?
[05:06] Luis Ortega: Capture: p50/p95 latency, batch sizes distribution, KV hit rate (by prefix vs session), per-route compute tokens, and failed fallbacks. We'll provide a prebuilt dashboard.
[05:17] Tom Reed: For the sandbox workload, can you simulate the long-tail 40-turn sessions without sending PII?
[05:22] Maya Chen: Yes we'll provide a synthetic generator; you can run it on sanitized logs. We'll also show how to instrument sampling so you can spot correctness regressions.
[05:30] Aisha Khan: Any rough runbook for tuning after the sandbox? Like stepwise TTL adjustments.
[05:34] Luis Ortega: Recommend three stages: baseline (no prefetch), staged prefetch (prefix only, conservative TTL), then hybrid (session-affine + prefix, tune TTLs downward if storage grows). Each stage run for 3–5 business days with monitoring.
[05:49] Priya Menon: What about eviction policy specifics — LRU vs LFU?
[05:52] Hannah Park: Default is TTL + LRU for session KV; for prefix caches we bias by access frequency and recency (LFU + decaying counts). You can set an eviction budget per-pool.
[06:03] Tom Reed: When would you recommend an aggressive approach?
[06:06] Luis Ortega: Aggressive when prefix flows are highly repeatable (like FAQ-driven chat) and storage is cheap relative to computed tokens; conservative if user churn is high and privacy constraints limit caching.
[06:17] Aisha Khan: Competitor question — LargeCloudAI claims they do zero-copy KV; how is Redwood different?
[06:22] Maya Chen: We benchmarked and zero-copy helps, but the bigger wins are routing + batching + TTL tuning together. Our console ties those levers and runs sims to show end-to-end savings rather than isolated tech claims.
[06:35] Tom Reed: Ok let's map responsibilities for the sandbox.
[06:38] Maya Chen: Action items we put in the sheet. I'll read them: Maya to share detailed cost workbook (due 02/23), Luis to provision sandbox and seed with synthetic workload (due 02/24), Priya to share peak QPS/time-of-day distribution and any PII constraints (due 02/23), Tom to confirm KMS policy and whether bring-your-own-key is allowed for test keys (due 02/25).
[06:58] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. Quick Q: can Optimize drive on-the-fly quantization changes or is that a manual model roll?
[07:04] Hannah Park: Model variant changes are through a rollout. Optimize can recommend quantization and point you to the compaction profile, but the actual variant swap is a deployment step — we support automated canary then traffic shift.
[07:16] Tom Reed: Will you include a recommended golden config we can apply in production after the sandbox?
[07:20] Luis Ortega: Yes — the workbook will include a 'recommended config' JSON snippet you can drop into your deployment configs. We'll also include an SDK snippet for client-side session affinity.
[07:29] Priya Menon: Anything else on compliance? We need egress logs and retention windows.
[07:34] Maya Chen: Retention windows are configurable per-tenant. Egress logs can be exported to your S3 or SIEM with KMS encryption. We'll send the policy doc.
[07:42] Aisha Khan: Great. Let's schedule the follow-up — how about 30 minutes next Thurs to review sandbox metrics?
[07:47] Maya Chen: Works for us, we'll propose slots. Thanks everyone.
[07:51] //end meeting notes - last 40 minutes had some QA and walkthrough of the workbook tabs, sandbox invite accepted by Priya//
[51:59] Transcript end: 15:52 UTC
notes: Meeting was cooperative; customer is risk-averse on KMS and data residency but motivated by cost savings. Sandbox will be key to proving the aggressive scenario. Luis to run a quick pre-sim overnight to sanity-check the workbook parameters.
